questions.stem: A 41 year old man has had a sudden onset of high fever, severe aching in his legs and back, headache and a dry cough since yesterday. It is January and several colleagues are off sick. His temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Abrupt high fever, severe myalgia, headache and dry cough in winter with a clear chest and tachycardia is influenza.

steps.x: **Abrupt** fever, **severe myalgia**, winter clustering, clear chest.

elim: A post-cold productive cough with mild fever, not abrupt high fever and severe myalgia.
Coryza with little fever or myalgia.
The chest is clear and saturation normal.
No rash, neck stiffness or shock.

steps.x: **D. Influenza.** Sudden fever + severe myalgia in winter = influenza.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman had influenza 8 days ago and was improving. Over 2 days she has developed high fever, pleuritic chest pain and a cough productive of purulent sputum. Her temperature is 39.6°C, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There are coarse lower zone crackles. Her CXR (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral lower zone consolidation with a right lower zone cavity.

questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza is classically Staph. aureus, which can cavitate.

clues: had influenza 8 days ago and was improving
steps.x: Biphasic illness: influenza then **bacterial pneumonia** with cavitation.

elim: From water systems, with hyponatraemia and diarrhoea.

steps.x: **E. Staphylococcus aureus.** Post-flu cavitating pneumonia = Staph. aureus.

questions.stem: Five adults in the same GP practice develop influenza during a winter outbreak. Each has fever, myalgia and dry cough.
questions.q: Which patient is at highest risk of complications?
o: A 30 year old woman with hay fever
A 34 year old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant
A 38 year old man who runs marathons
A 45 year old man with a previous appendicectomy
questions.e: Risk factors for complicated influenza are older age, chronic disease, pregnancy and immunosuppression.

steps.x: Look for **pregnancy, age, chronic disease, immunosuppression**.
**C. A 34 year old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant.** Pregnancy = high risk.

questions.stem: A novel influenza A virus spreads rapidly across several continents within months. It carries a haemagglutinin subtype that has not circulated in humans for decades, and most of the population has no immunity.
questions.q: Which process is most likely responsible for this new strain?
questions.e: Antigenic shift produces novel HA/NA antigens to which the population has little immunity, causing pandemics.

clues: haemagglutinin subtype that has not circulated
steps.x: A **novel subtype** causing a **pandemic**.

elim: Gradual point mutations causing seasonal epidemics, not novel subtypes.

steps.x: **B. Antigenic shift.** New subtype + pandemic = shift.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had his influenza vaccine last autumn. This winter he develops fever, myalgia and dry cough, and PCR confirms influenza A of the same subtype. Laboratory analysis shows several point mutations in the haemagglutinin gene compared with the vaccine strain.
questions.q: Which process explains why the vaccine did not protect him?
questions.e: Drift is gradual point mutation in HA/NA giving partial immune evasion and seasonal epidemics, so the vaccine is updated annually.

steps.x: Same subtype, **point mutations**.

elim: Shift produces a new subtype; this is the same subtype with point mutations.
Not a cause of vaccine failure.

steps.x: **A. Antigenic drift.** Point mutations = drift.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has had influenza for 4 days. He now has central chest pain worse on lying flat, palpitations and breathlessness. His pulse rate is 126 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with widespread T-wave changes. Troponin is raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Chest pain, palpitations, tachycardia and raised troponin after influenza point to myocarditis.

steps.x: Young man, **viral** illness, cardiac pain with raised troponin.

elim: Young, no risk factors, after a viral illness.
Would give pleuritic pain and hypoxia, not widespread T changes.
No productive cough or focal signs.

steps.x: **B. Myocarditis.** Post-flu chest pain + troponin = myocarditis.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl had influenza 5 days ago. She now has right ear pain and a fever of 38.4°C. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging tympanic membrane.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Influenza can be complicated by otitis media, as well as sinusitis, myocarditis and PE.

steps.x: A **bulging red drum** after flu.

elim: Affects the canal, with a normal drum.

steps.x: **A. Acute otitis media.** Bulging drum = otitis media.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with diabetes has had influenza for 5 days. Today she has new breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chest pain, breathlessness or hypoxia after influenza should raise suspicion of secondary bacterial pneumonia as an emergency.

clues: coarse crackles at the left base
steps.x: Influenza with **hypoxia**, chest pain and **focal** crackles.

elim: Would not cause hypoxia and focal crackles.
No asthma; focal crackles not wheeze.
Bilateral crackles, not focal with fever.
Chest exam is usually normal and saturation normal.

steps.x: **D. Secondary bacterial pneumonia.** Flu + hypoxia + focal signs = bacterial pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has been bed-bound with influenza for 6 days. He suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness and coughs up blood. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 108/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. His chest is clear and his left calf is swollen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Influenza can be complicated by PE (SOB, chest pain, haemoptysis), especially with immobility.

steps.x: Sudden pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, **clear chest**, **DVT**.
**C. Pulmonary embolism.** Flu + immobility + haemoptysis = PE.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has had fever, headache, sore throat and severe muscle aches for 2 days. Her temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. Her chest is clear. A nasopharyngeal swab PCR detects an enveloped virus with a segmented RNA genome.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Influenza virus (type A or B) is an enveloped virus with a segmented RNA genome.

steps.x: Myalgic febrile illness from a **segmented RNA** virus.
**B. Influenza B virus.** Segmented RNA genome = influenza.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with COPD has had abrupt fever, myalgia and dry cough for 1 day. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: The gold standard for influenza is a nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR.

clues: abrupt fever, myalgia and dry cough
steps.x: High-risk patient; confirm before antivirals.
**C. Nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR.** Gold standard: NP swab PCR.

questions.stem: A 27 year old healthy woman has had abrupt fever, headache, severe myalgia and dry cough for 1 day. Public Health has reported high community circulation of influenza. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to diagnosis?
questions.e: In healthy adults during high community circulation, influenza can be diagnosed clinically.

steps.x: **Healthy** adult during **high circulation**.

elim: Not needed with a clear chest.
Not needed in a healthy adult during high circulation.

steps.x: **B. Clinical diagnosis without testing.** Clinical diagnosis is enough.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man on azathioprine after a kidney transplant has had fever, myalgia and dry cough for 1 day during a flu season. His temperature is 38.5°C and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Immunosuppressed patients should have the diagnosis confirmed with nasopharyngeal viral PCR.

steps.x: **Immunosuppressed**, so a clinical diagnosis is not enough.

elim: Clinical diagnosis is for healthy adults; he is immunosuppressed.

steps.x: **C. Nasopharyngeal swab for viral PCR.** High-risk = confirm with PCR.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has had fever, myalgia and dry cough for 2 days during a flu outbreak. He has no medical history. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult is managed supportively.

steps.x: **Healthy** adult, uncomplicated.

elim: Postpone when acutely unwell; vaccines prevent, not treat.

steps.x: **D. Rest, fluids and paracetamol.** Supportive care.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with heart failure has had sudden fever, myalgia and dry cough for 1 day during a local influenza outbreak. PCR confirms influenza A. Her temperature is 38.6°C and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: High-risk patients (heart failure) get first-line oral oseltamivir (or inhaled zanamivir).

steps.x: Confirmed flu in a **high-risk** patient.
**C. Oral oseltamivir.** High risk = oseltamivir.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with chronic liver disease has confirmed influenza. She cannot take oral oseltamivir because of resistance in the circulating strain. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative?
questions.e: Inhaled zanamivir is the alternative neuraminidase inhibitor for high-risk patients.

steps.x: High risk, oseltamivir unsuitable.
**A. Inhaled zanamivir.** Zanamivir is the other neuraminidase inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with diabetes has had influenza for 3 days. He is now increasingly breathless. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows no consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Respiratory failure (low saturation, tachypnoea) in influenza needs admission for IV antiviral therapy, with ICU if ventilation is needed.

steps.x: **Respiratory failure** from influenza.

elim: No bacterial pneumonia and he needs admission.

steps.x: **A. Admit for intravenous antiviral therapy.** Respiratory failure = admit for IV antiviral.

questions.stem: A 38 year old nurse who works on a haematology ward asks her occupational health department about influenza vaccination. She has no medical history.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: No vaccine as she is under 65
questions.e: Healthcare workers should have an annual influenza vaccine; the standard IM vaccine contains inactivated virus.

steps.x: **Healthcare worker** near immunosuppressed patients.

elim: Live vaccine is for children; needed annually.

steps.x: **A. Annual inactivated influenza vaccine.** Healthcare workers: annual vaccine.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with COPD attends a flu vaccine clinic. He has had a fever of 38.5°C and a productive cough for 2 days. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate action?
o: Give a double dose of vaccine
Give the vaccine and start antibiotics
Never vaccinate him because of COPD
Postpone vaccination until he has recovered
questions.e: Postpone vaccination if acutely unwell until recovered.

steps.x: Eligible but **acutely unwell**.

elim: COPD is an indication for vaccination.

steps.x: **E. Postpone vaccination until he has recovered.** Unwell = postpone.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with no medical history attends her GP surgery in October 2025 for her seasonal influenza vaccine.
questions.q: Which vaccine is most appropriate?
o: No vaccine until she develops a chronic disease
questions.e: For 2025/2026, people aged 65 and over are offered aTIV, high-dose TIV/QIV or recombinant TIVr/QIVr.

steps.x: Aged **65 or over** in 2025/26.

elim: Age 65 or over is an indication alone.

steps.x: **A. Adjuvanted trivalent inactivated vaccine (aTIV).** Over 65: aTIV (or high-dose or recombinant).

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant asks her midwife whether she should have the influenza vaccine. She has asthma and is worried about a vaccine containing live virus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: Pregnant women should have the annual inactivated (killed) influenza vaccine, safe in comorbidities.

steps.x: **Pregnancy** is an indication; the IM vaccine is **inactivated**.

elim: Inactivated flu vaccine is recommended in pregnancy.
Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy.
Pregnant women are offered it at any stage.

steps.x: **B. Have the inactivated vaccine now.** Pregnant = inactivated vaccine now.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has influenza A. A student asks which viral protein allows the virus to attach to respiratory epithelial cells.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of attachment?
o: Haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors
questions.e: Influenza enters via haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors.

steps.x: **Attachment** protein of influenza.
**B. Haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid receptors.** HA binds sialic acid.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with influenza is given oseltamivir. A student asks how it shortens her illness.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of oseltamivir?
o: Prevents release of new virions from infected cells
questions.e: Neuraminidase releases new virions; inhibitors like oseltamivir block this.

steps.x: Oseltamivir is a **neuraminidase inhibitor**.
**E. Prevents release of new virions from infected cells.** Blocks virion release.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man develops pneumococcal pneumonia 6 days after influenza. A student asks why influenza made bacterial pneumonia more likely.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Antibodies to influenza cross-react with bacteria
Damaged respiratory epithelium impairs mucociliary clearance
Influenza virus produces a bacterial toxin
questions.e: Influenza destroys respiratory epithelium, impairing mucociliary clearance and predisposing to Staph. aureus or Strep. pneumoniae.

steps.x: Why does **flu** open the door to bacteria?
**B. Damaged respiratory epithelium impairs mucociliary clearance.** Epithelial damage impairs mucociliary clearance.
